doc.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998

title: Norman Granz and concept albums
summary: Contrasting Granz's record-and-release approach with conceived albums, later the Ella Fitzgerald Songbooks.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Well that’s true you had to do that in order to stand out. Now I don’t like to talk against competition but take Norman Granz’s operation which was eventually the Verve label and all. Norman made a tremendous number of records but his approach was basically to just bring the guys into the studio or record them on stage, and then figure out what to do about packaging and there was never any really concept in any of the albums. I’m sorry to single out Norman, but it’s an easy target for this idea of you can go two ways. Just record artists and put the records out hoping that something will hit, and then the other way is to try to record them in a way in which there is an idea behind it which will attract the customer. Eventually, since I — I shouldn’t have done this but it’s not being publicly broadcast so I don’t feel so bad — I will say this that Norman ended up recognizing this and that’s when he got into the series of the Ella Fitzgerald Songbook, Ella sings Richard Rodgers and so on and so on. Those were the pop conceptions that other people like myself were doing a long time ago. And it worked very well so that these are now classic © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-
albums that have an identity and significance within simply themselves, instead of just being part of the body of work of an artist.
